definition.text: An animal adapted to eat plants, such as leaves, fruits or seeds, as the main part of its diet.

facts.text: Herbivores are primary consumers: they eat the carbohydrates plants make by photosynthesis, and carnivores in turn eat them.
Many rely on gut bacteria and protozoans to break down cellulose, which is much harder to digest than animal tissue.
Herbivory shapes plant diversity: abundant deer reduce plant species richness, while bison hold back dominant plants so others can flourish.
When predators decline, unchecked herbivores can over-forage and suppress plant communities.
Over-browsing by white-tailed deer in the US could cost forest restoration projects more than $750 million a year.
Some herbivory is mutualistic: seed dispersal and pollination feed the animal while helping the plant reproduce.

definition.text: The two main herbivore feeding strategies: grazers such as cows eat mostly grass, while browsers such as moose eat tree leaves and twigs.

facts.text: A land mammal counts as a grazer if at least 90% of its forage is grass, and a browser if at least 90% is tree leaves and twigs; in between is mixed-feeding.
Small herbivores pick high-quality forage, while larger ones are less selective.
Kleiber's law says larger animals need less food per unit of body weight than smaller ones.

definition.text: A plant trait that improves its survival or reproduction when animals feed on it.

facts.text: Defenses fall into tolerance, withstanding damage without losing fitness, and resistance, reducing how much damage is done.
Herbivores counter defenses by choosing which plants to eat, adapting their own bodies, or modifying the plant.
Many herbivores eat a mix of plants to balance nutrients and avoid too much of any one defensive chemical.

definition.text: An organism that cannot make its own food and instead gets its carbon from other organisms or their remains.

facts.text: Heterotrophs include most animals, all fungi, some bacteria and protists, and many parasitic plants.
In a food chain they are the consumers, while autotrophs, which make food from sunlight or inorganic chemicals, are the producers.
Detritivores are heterotrophs that eat dead plant and animal matter and feces.
Respiration by heterotrophic microbes releases much of the CO2 entering the atmosphere, which plants then reuse.
By mineralization they convert organic nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus into inorganic forms plants can use, which is critical to plant survival and soil fertility.
